📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, becky the basset hound is giving new meaning to the term “man’s best friend.” On November 12, she walked to the Whiteface Lodge, a ski resort in Lake Placid, New York. The hotel staff immediately recognized the dog, but not because of her sparkling personality or floppy ears. Becky’s owner has dementia, and the unnamed man has disappeared before.

According to recent reports, the team at Whiteface called the New York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search. Four NYSP officers and 14 Rangers used drones and another dog (a bloodhound) to search for the missing person. According to Charlie Foutch, the lead Ranger on the search, it was about 25 to 30 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.

Industry observers note that at 10 a.m. the next morning, a hunter who was searching just ahead of the group heard someone fall and scream. He found the missing man off to the side of a trail in a draining area with open woods. Ranger Sabo arrived on the scene shortly after. The 69-year-old man was not wearing gloves or shoes, and was suffering from some frostbite on his feet and hands. He was still alert and talking.

“We’re always looking for live people. That’s our goal is to find a live person,” remarked Fouch. “And a lot of people are really tough. This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning or mittens or gloves, so he had been out there for some period of time at night. And he still did okay. Sometimes if you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do okay.”.

Due to his injuries and the location off the trail, a hoist was the safest and quickest way to get him to safety. Ranger Martin used a cable to hoist him up to a helicopter, while NYSP Pilot Engle flew them to the hospital.

In addition to this coordination between hunters, the NYSP, and DEC, Fouch said that Becky the basset hound made this happy ending possible.

According to recent reports, “I think if the dog had not shown up at Whiteface, that gentleman definitely would have had a different outcome,” said Fouch. “It definitely would have been much harder to find him. He may not have survived the rest of the day and probably not another night. The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so swiftly.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in Latest York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein.
  • According to recent reports, pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint.
  • Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in Latest York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein. Pawson, then an architectural wunderkind from the United Kingdom, and Smith-Petersen, a young Danish-Italian communications manager for the fashion house, found themselves collaborating on the opening of the brand’s first flagship on Madison Avenue.

According to recent reports, pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint. His earliest residential works (a Mallorca summer house for collectors, an art dealer’s London apartment) provided a series of simple surfaces, plinths, and frames—for objects, for vistas, and for life. The same was true at the Calvin Klein store, where designer and client amplified each other’s design approaches in a meeting of minimalist minds.

Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.

The living area features a table and chairs by Poul Kjærholm.

A sauna is clad in blackened wood.

It has been revealed that pawson’s recent residence for Smith-Petersen and her husband, Enrico Erba Springorum, an Armani executive, makes another case for life with less. “The imprint came from childhood: the minimalism, the Danish design,” explains Smith-Petersen, who grew up outside Copenhagen. “Poul Kjærholm was our neighbor,” she adds, name-checking the widely influential midcentury modernist. There were also formative summers spent at the pared-back house her father designed on the Turkish peninsula of Çeşme. About the location, she recalls, “People stated, ‘You guys are crazy!’ But it was a place close to nature and the sea. And then later it became a destination.”.

A single sculptural tree dots the courtyard.

An oak bed with integrated bedside tables anchors the primary bedroom.

Recent findings suggest that ninety minutes south of Milan, the patchwork hills of the Val Luretta are far less isolated. Its proximity to the city has attracted editors, artists, and other creatives in search of space and quiet. That tranquility drew Smith-Petersen to the area when she was seeking land on which to build a compound with her younger brother, Henrik, for their families. (She and her husband have two adult sons.) Over the years, she and Pawson had maintained a friendship. “So when Henrik and I found the property, I had this crazy idea: Why don’t I ask John?” indicates Smith-Petersen. “My brother noted, ‘Forget it!’ But we went to visit John and his team in London and it kicked off from there.”.

The primary bath’s bespoke vanity, topped in a Grassi Pietri surface.

Smith-Petersen stands in the living area.

A view across the dining table toward the minimalist hearth.

The resulting structure, realized with project architect Giulio Marchesi, is the irst of two planned homes on the site, one for each sibling. Sitting long and low on the land, like an ivory piano key dropped onto the hillside, the single-story house frames expansive views of the Val Luretta. “The area of the countryside is so dramatic,” reflects Pawson, whose first visit to the site was in winter fog. “In the summer, it’s very different—it’s so lush.”.

According to recent reports, at some 2,500 square feet, the house is spacious but intimate, with Pawson’s trademark spareness and remarkable warmth. He designed it along one axis, a long corridor connecting the foyer to the open-plan kitchen, dining area, and living area, then bedrooms beyond. White-painted plaster walls and floors of pale-gray stone, sourced nearby in Vicenza, radiate calm. As Pawson explains, understanding the way the body and the eye move through a space is paramount—and can take time. “You’ve got to learn the choreography,” he notes. Living in and feeling the house is key.

Smith-Petersen and Pawson on-site.

The yearslong friendship Pawson and Smith-Petersen had forged helped him understand how she would use the space. There would be mornings at the Pawson-designed table, afternoons on the terrace or under one of the century-old oaks, and evenings making dinner in a kitchen brimming with Scandinavian tableware. In solitude or surrounded by family, there’s complete peace on offer.

The open-plan dining area and kitchen.

“Most architects—contemporaries, colleagues—always say, ‘Oh, it’s impossible, a private house,’ ” says Pawson. The process can be “very emotional. And that’s what makes it good.” Luckily for Smith-Petersen, the primary feeling the house evokes is serenity. “I didn’t expect to be in such awe,” she says. “I was never a country person. Sometimes, I try to arrive a day before anyone else is here and do a silent retreat,” she adds. “It’s where I feel best now. It’s pure joy.”.

In the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S. government to stop supersonic jets. By day, the Harvard-trained physicist ran experiments at the Cambridge Electron Accelerator. By night, he spent hours writing letters—to congressmen, federal aviation officials, mayors, and newspaper editors. It was not a job he wanted. “I was hoping and praying someone else would do it,” he told The Harvard Crimson.

Sources indicate that but no one else would. So Shurcliff rolled out the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S. commercial aviation history at the time, the Supersonic Transport (SST) program. His opposition to the SST stemmed from research by Swedish scientist Bo Lundberg, who had written extensively on the perils of supersonic aviation, chiefly the sonic boom, which could impact hundreds of millions of people every day. Shurcliff’s goal was uncompromising. “Just as the only way to get rid of the smell of the skunk is to eliminate the skunk,” he told The Newly introduced York Times, “we propose to attack the sonic boom by eliminating the SST.”.

It worked. In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S. soil.

It has been revealed that today, prompted by a 2025 executive order, the FAA is proposing to lift that ban before any community response tests of emerging supersonic technology have taken place. And even if new engineering designs can reduce the sonic booms at airliner scale, the economic and environmental costs that have plagued supersonic flight haven’t changed since Shurcliff’s day.

Sources indicate that during World War II, Shurcliff worked at the federal Office of Scientific Research and Development, helping keep the Manhattan Project’s atomic-bomb patents secret. In 1946, he witnessed firsthand the atomic tests at Bikini Atoll and wrote the official account, Bombs at Bikini. His son later told The New York Times that his father was so affected he spent the rest of his life atoning for that work.

It has been revealed that when supersonic aviation programs began heating up in the 1960s, Shurcliff was wary of the press, but he was clear about supersonic technology. “We all believe in progress,” he told the Crimson, “but some things just aren’t progress.”.

The U.S. government-sponsored SST program was the culmination of supersonic military research that began on the heels of World War II. In January 1947, months before anyone had flown faster than sound, Popular Science described Bell’s experimental XS-1, also known as the X-1, which it said might someday reach 1,700 mph, more than twice the speed of sound and three times faster than a typical commercial jet. That October, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier in the X-1.

According to recent reports, fifteen years later, in 1962, Britain and France agreed to build Concorde, and the Soviet Union soon rolled out its own supersonic airliner program, Tupolev Tu-144. The following year, President John F. Kennedy committed the U.S. to a faster, bigger rival, SST. Boeing won the contract in 1966. But even as the race heated up, an enormous problem trailed in its wake.

Recent findings suggest that sit in a closed room and the air feels perfectly still, but it isn’t. At room temperature, air molecules zip around at an average of about 1,000 miles per hour, each one bouncing off its neighbors billions of times a second. You don’t feel a gale because they’re flying every which way at once—for every molecule headed toward your face, another is headed away. What you’re feeling, without noticing, is the sum of all that pummeling—air pressure—about 14.7 pounds of it on every square inch (psi) of your body at sea level. You notice it only when the balance shifts, such as when the wind blows—a mass of air being pushed from high pressure toward low.

That restless jostling of air molecules is also how sound travels. A voice, a drumbeat, or a jet engine will shove the molecules, which pass along the shove like a crowd in a stadium passing along a wave even as every fan stays in place. The ricocheting molecules pass along vibrations somewhat inefficiently, which is why sound travels a bit slower than the molecules themselves, about 760 mph at sea level, and slower still in the frigid air at airplane cruising altitudes.

In a recent development, when a plane flies faster than the speed of sound, it outruns the air molecules carrying the wave. The air ahead gets no warning until the jet slams it aside, compressing it and creating a shock wave that trails the jet like the V-shaped wake behind a speedboat. But the shock wave’s wake is three-dimensional, spreading in a widening cone that sweeps across the ground below.

It has been revealed that A sonic boom isn’t a single bang that occurs the moment a plane “breaks the sound barrier.” It’s a continuous swath of jarring noise and pressure that follows the jet. Anyone in the cone’s path, or “boom carpet,” experiences it.

Recent findings suggest that in his 1970 explainer, S/S/T and Sonic Boom Handbook, Shurcliff estimated the boom carpet at 40 to 60 miles wide for the supersonic aircraft of his day. The jolt hits hardest directly beneath the flight path and weakens toward the cone’s edges.

In a recent development, worse, Shurcliff warned, boom behavior was erratic. Swirls of wind and temperature could focus a shock wave so that one house took twice the jolt of its neighbor a few hundred feet away. That, he argued, meant people would never get used to sonic booms, just as people never get used to lightning and thunder.

On paper, booms don’t seem like they should be a substantial deal. A boom from supersonic passenger jets like Concorde raises air pressure at sea level about .014 psi relative to the normal 14.7 psi we live with—that’s just a 0.1 percent increase. It doesn’t seem like much, but relative to everyday sounds, it’s enormous.

Industry observers note that if you’ve ever stood near the speakers at a live concert and felt the bass or drum hit your chest, you’ve felt a pressure pulse like a sonic boom, but that bass is only 6.5 pascals, or Pa, a measure of air pressure. Now multiply that punch by about 15 and deliver it without warning. It’s roughly the shove of a 30 mph wind gust delivered in a fraction of a second and aimed at every wall and window of your house at once. That’s what the 0.1 percent of a supersonic jet actually represents.

What no one knew in the early 1960s, when supersonic research was barreling ahead, was how people would feel living under that boom carpet day after day. In 1964, the FAA decided to find out, picking Oklahoma City.

It has been revealed that in a six-month trial that began in February 1964, Oklahoma City residents were subjected to eight sonic booms a day, starting at 7 a.m., to gauge how well they would accept the disruption, and whether they would grow accustomed to it. By the end, the Oklahoma City Council had requested a halt to the flights, and the FAA had logged more than 12,000 calls, mostly complaints, alongside more than 5,000 damage claims for broken windows, cracked walls and floors, and destruction of personal property.

Despite the fallout, the following year the agency pointed to a University of Chicago survey of Oklahoma City residents as vindication. Nearly three-quarters remarked they could live with eight booms a day indefinitely. The survey’s own numbers told a different story.

Nearly every resident surveyed, 94 percent, reported rattling walls and windows, and almost four in 10 believed the booms had damaged their homes. The longer the booms continued, the less people liked them. The share who felt more than a little annoyed rose from 37 percent to 56 percent, and those who remarked they could live with the booms fell from 91 percent to 73 percent during the six-month trial. Anger over the FAA’s handling of damage claims eventually turned Oklahoma Senator Mike Monroney, one of aviation’s staunchest champions, against the SST program.

Sources indicate that although the residents of Oklahoma City delivered mixed results, the negative data emboldened the opposition. Shurcliff released the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom (CLASB) in March 1967 with a handful of friends and colleagues. Their mission was to eliminate the SST program and keep its boom out of American skies. By June, CLASB had about 230 members in 18 states. What united them, Shurcliff told The Newly introduced York Times, was that they were “human beings who don’t like to be hit over our heads without our permission being asked.”.

Recent findings suggest that SST opposition grew as the fight dragged on. Environmental groups joined in, along with economists who doubted the SST would ever pay for itself. For a man new to public relations, Shurcliff seized the moment, casting sonic booms in the language of a rising environmental movement, calling them “sonic pollution.” Atmospheric scientists began warning that SST’s high-altitude exhaust could erode the ozone layer.

In a recent development, in 1971, Congress finally voted to cut off the program’s funding, ending America’s bid for a supersonic passenger airliner. But across the Atlantic, the European program was forging ahead.

It has been revealed that in 1963, a plane flew to space. Why couldn’t we go farther?

In 1934, Chrysler bet big on teardrop-shaped cars.

It has been revealed that robotaxis almost happened in 1964—with help from the U.S. government.

According to recent reports, in 1871, cities almost got moving sidewalks. Why are we still waiting?

During WWI, a daredevil pilot helped invent the first ‘drones’.

It has been revealed that in 1916, hybrid cars could’ve changed history. But Ford wouldn’t allow it.

Concorde began carrying paying passengers in January 1976, cruising at twice the speed of sound and crossing the Atlantic in about three and a half hours. But the U.S. overland ban confined it mostly to ocean routes. Only British Airways and Air France, both state-owned at the time, ever flew Concorde’s small fleet.

In July 2000, an Air France Concorde flight crashed on takeoff outside Paris, killing everyone aboard and halting flights for more than a year. In February 2002, Popular Science writer Bill Sweetman called the crash not only a tragedy but also “a metaphor for the sorry state of supersonic air travel.” But he also reported that a new supersonic race had “quietly” begun.

Sources indicate that private-jet maker Gulfstream wanted “a passenger jet for the rich that can smash the sound barrier yet is quiet enough to fly anywhere, anytime.” Controlling the boom was the chief obstacle. But in August 2003, over the California desert, a modified Northrop Grumman F-5 fighter plane demonstrated that a sonic boom could be reshaped and softened.

Two months later, Concorde made its last commercial flight, officially ending the supersonic era for passenger airliners.

Sources indicate that the modern darling of supersonic flight is NASA’s X-59, a one-seat research jet built by Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works. With a tapered nose that stretches roughly a third of its length, the plane’s shape spreads the shock waves so they reach the ground as a thump rather than a boom. The X-59 first flew in October 2025, went supersonic in June 2026, and a week later reached its target of Mach 1.4, or roughly 925 mph at 55,000 feet. Next, NASA intends to fly it over U.S. communities and ask residents how the thumps sound to them. In effect, we’re gearing up for Oklahoma City again, six decades later, albeit, with a gentler jolt.

Since Concorde’s retirement, a handful of private supersonic startups have come, and mostly gone. Denver-based Boom Supersonic flew its one-third-scale XB-1 demonstrator faster than sound three times in January 2025, claiming that no audible boom reached the ground. Its engineering innovation is to exploit atmospheric physics. Since sound travels faster in warm air near the ground than in the frigid air up high, a jet flying only slightly faster than sound at altitude is effectively flying slower than sound near the surface. So its shock waves bend back upward before they land, a phenomenon called Mach cutoff. Boom’s planned Overture jet, seating 60 to 80 passengers, would cruise at Mach 1.7 over oceans—leaving booms in its wake—but just above Mach 1 over land, where their booms would never be heard on the ground, just the distant rumble of their jet engines. The plane hasn’t been built, and its engine is still in development.

But Washington isn’t waiting for the data. A June 2025 executive order directed the FAA to repeal its 1973 sonic boom ban over land. In July 2026, the agency proposed a replacement. Civilian jets, both commercial and private, could fly supersonic over U.S. soil as long as their booms register no more than 0.11 pounds per square foot on the ground, about a twentieth of Concorde’s. That’s about 5 Pa, or slightly less than the pressure felt standing next to the speakers at a live concert (6.5 Pa). But airlines, airports, and Europe’s aviation regulator have questioned whether enough evidence supports the number, which the FAA set without the X-59 having flown over a single community.

Recent findings suggest that even if the boom fades to a thump, the environmental cost doesn’t. Flying faster than sound means fighting far more drag. According to a 2018 analysis by the International Council on Clean Transportation, a new supersonic airliner would “burn five to seven times as much fuel per passenger as a comparable subsonic jet.” Boom Supersonic says Overture will be able to run entirely on sustainable aviation fuel, but airlines, not manufacturers, decide what goes in the tank.

As Popular Science’s Bill Sweetman wrote in 2002, if you can afford a supersonic jet, “you’re not worried about a few lousy tons of fuel.” But everyone below will bear the cost of supersonic jetsetters’ small travel-time benefit in excess noise and climate-warming emissions.

Shurcliff saw this attempt to relax the rules coming. “Once they start flying, they’re going to want to fly them everywhere,” he told The Upcoming York Times in 1967, warning that over-water routes would be “like a foot in the door.” Fifty-nine years later, thanks to the FAA, the door is swinging open. It’s up to us to decide whether we’re prepared to live with the repercussions or push back as Shurcliff did more than half a century ago.

#133866. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.
  • The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.
  • Both measures were linked to mortality risk and indicated similar ability to predict it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and indicated similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

Sources indicate that it included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

In a recent development, from this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:.

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

Industry observers note that the study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own highlighted modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Industry observers note that several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

In a recent development, overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

Recent findings suggest that “Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”.

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she noted. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she stated.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” mentioned Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he mentioned. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

According to recent reports, “I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he stated. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth.
  • William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth. The probe reached this record-breaking milestone at approximately 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, November 18. Since takes about 24 hours to receive any signal from Voyager 1, NASA officially confirmed that it reached the distance on Thursday, November 19.

William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

According to recent reports, “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he claims. “They show that we are explorers and can work together to do wonderful things.”.

Industry observers note that astronomers often describe vast cosmic distances in light-years. It’s arguably the most famous unit of measurement when talking about the universe, in part because of its sheer incomprehensibility. A single particle of light travels at a speed of about 186,282 miles per second. Hypothetically speaking, if you fired a beam of light into the night sky at the outset of reading this story, it would travel around 44.7 million miles into space by the time you finished.

But even a unit like a light-minute isn’t particularly useful to astronomers. For them, cosmic measurements only start making sense on a scale of light-years. Voyager 1 is nowhere close to a light-year away from Earth, but a light-day (approximately 16,094,799,105 miles) is still basically impossible to envision as a distance. And since radio communications travel at nearly the speed of light, any messages to and from the spacecraft will require about 24 (Earth) hours to receive.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” Dave Gallagher, the director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, mentioned in an emailed statement confirming the milestone. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”.

Even at one light-day from Earth, Voyager 1 isn’t done just yet. While several of its instruments are no longer functioning, it still routinely sends back invaluable information from its vantage point beyond the solar system.

Sources indicate that “Voyager 1 is telling us about our sun’s interaction with its galactic neighborhood. It has told us about the amount of galactic cosmic rays, unfiltered by the sun’s magnetic field,” says Kurth. “We are learning about the variation of plasma density in the interstellar medium just outside the heliosphere (sun’s extended atmosphere). We’re anxious to see where the direction of the magnetic field rotates from one similar to the heliospheric direction to that of the pristine interstellar medium.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Though it might be a long shot, I hope to see Voyager 1 crossing into the predicted hot hydrogen wall,” Adam Szabo, a Project Investigator on Voyager’s Magnetometer Experiment, tells Popular Science. “The wall is composed of neutral hydrogen atoms, so it will not register easily, but it must have some magnetic and plasma wave signature.”.

It has been revealed that voyager 1 rolled out on September 5, 1977, heading for Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 has 10 scientific instruments onboard, including two Golden Records engraved with sights, sounds, and depictions of life on Earth onboard—should the probe encounter any extraterrestrial life.

In a recent development, in March 1979, the Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two newly introduced Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis. When it reached Saturn in 1980, the spacecraft spotted five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.

Sources indicate that as part of a concept that NASA called the Grand Tour, the Voyager mission as a whole took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. Its twin spacecraft Voyager 2 later explored Neptune and Uranus.

On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 became the furthest human-made object in space, after overtaking NASA’s Pioneer 10 probe. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, and became the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere. This boundary is where the influences from outside of our solar system are stronger than those from our sun.

All good things must come to an end, of course. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by decaying plutonium-23. The isotope possesses a 87.74-year half-life, so the batteries are presently operating at around two-thirds their original strength. NASA has slowly shut down onboard equipment in recent years to conserve energy, but there will come a time when there simply isn’t enough left in the RTGs for anything to operate. Barring any technical issues, mission engineers expect to bid Voyager 1 a final farewell sometime during the 2030s.

The spacecraft may cease its work as a cosmic laboratory, but its very existence ensures it will remain a monument to humanity’s potential as it barrels forward for eons.

“Voyager 1 and its companion Voyager 2 have taught us time and again that nature is not as simple and predictable as we thought,” Kurth explains. “Voyager has always provided surprising differences from our best guesses as to what it will see in any new region.”.

Additionally, Szabo adds that it has an important lesson for anyone on Earth who has ever had a dream.

It has been revealed that “Do not be afraid to dream significant. In 1977, even the Grand Tour seemed like a long shot,” he notes. “We did not even conceive of making it into interstellar space. Dream big.”.

According to recent reports, UPGRADE November 19 10:00 a.m. EST: An earlier version of this story said light moves at 186,282 feet per second. It is 186,282 miles per second. We have updated unit of measurement and apologize for the error.

Bob Hope at Home: 10 Photos of the Comic’s Life Behind the Curtain

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that though Bob Hope was born in England, he fell in love with the USA.
  • Born Leslie Townes Hope in Eltham, London, on May 29, 1903, the future comedian and actor came from humble beginnings.
  • Below, we’ve rounded up 10 photos of Hope at home, from his early family life to the residence where he died at age 100.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that though Bob Hope was born in England, he fell in love with the USA. “Sometimes I do my best to hide it, but I’ve got a real crush on America,” he wrote in his 1990 memoir, Don’t Shoot, It’s Only Me. “Nobody ever had a girl like her. Nobody ever gave me as much affection, as much honor, or as much real estate.”.

Born Leslie Townes Hope in Eltham, London, on May 29, 1903, the future comedian and actor came from humble beginnings. His family had little money and moved often throughout his childhood. After he found success on stage and it came time to raise his own brood, Hope put down roots in California. Across Toluca Lake and Palm Springs, the star’s homes offered a place to escape the limelight, spend time with his wife and four kids, entertain very famous guests, and indulge in his love of golf.

Below, we’ve rounded up 10 photos of Hope at home, from his early family life to the residence where he died at age 100.

In a recent development, hope (bottom right) at the family estate in Cleveland. The comic’s parents William Henry Hope and Avis Townes Hope are on the porch in the background. Hope was 20 years old at the time of the picture.

Sources indicate that hope and his family moved from London to the United States when he was four. In this 1923 photo, he’s pictured with friends and members of the Hope clan at their Cleveland home. Because money was tight, the family took in boarders to supplement Hope’s father’s income, according to the Library of Congress. In his 1954 memoir, Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope recalls his early days in Cleveland. “The first place we lived by ourselves was Standiforth Court,” he wrote. “We were always on the move. We lived at 2029 Euclid. After that we moved behind the Cleveland Express barns…. It was a long walk between the barns and our house. And if we got home after dark, it was scary…. Next we lived at 1925 East 105th, then at 1913, then at 2029—all on Euclid. We didn’t move very far, only to bigger houses which had more room for roomers.”.

Hope and his wife Dolores at home in the 1940s.

Recent findings suggest that hope married Dolores DeFina in 1934, and the couple adopted their first child, a daughter named Linda, in 1939. That same year, the comic bought a five-acre former walnut grove in Los Angeles’s Toluca Lake neighborhood at 10346 Moorpark Street. He transformed the property into a lavish French Revival estate, featuring a 14,876-square-foot main house with eight bedrooms and eight bathrooms; a two-bedroom, two-bathroom guesthouse; a staff residence; and a pool.

Hope and his grandfather catch up over tea.

Industry observers note that in this 1943 photo, Hope is pictured at home with his “Grandpop.” As a young boy in London, Hope lived with his family in a house his grandfather had built. “Grandpop had built a row of houses in Eltham. We lived in one of them. They were put together like stone battleships,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. After moving to the United States, his grandfather went on to build churches in Cleveland and Detroit. Hope reunited with him during a return trip to England in 1939—the star’s first visit since moving across the pond as a child. He recalls the occasion in his memoir, writing that “It wasn’t until I went back to England in 1939 that I got to know [Grandpop]. It was the first time I’d been there since I was four. The English papers reported: ‘One-time shoeshine boy and ironmonger’s assistant comes home.’ The English are supposed to be conservative and not given to exaggeration, but they hooked one there. How could I have been a shoeshine boy or ironmonger’s assistant when I was only four when I left there?”.

Hope and family at home in the 1940s.

Industry observers note that back in California, Hope and his wife continued to grow their family. They adopted three more children: Anthony, born in 1940, and twins William and Eleanora, born in 1946. In this circa 1940s photo, the family of six is pictured at home. In Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope reflects on the choice to adopt. “No matter how strongly I feel about the word ‘family,’ Dolores feels even more deeply about it,” he writes. “When we found out that she couldn’t bear children, she began to bend my ear about adoption.” They welcomed their children through The Cradle, an adoption agency in Evanston, Illinois. “Of the five thousand, four hundred and nine babies that The Cradle has placed, there are eight Cradle babies out here in Hollywood,” he continues. “The Hopes are proud to be Cradle parents. I wish I could really tell you what The Cradle means to me here in Hollywood, where all day long the talk is box-office and autographs and premieres and who’ll get the Oscar. ‘The town of make-believe,’ they call it, but don’t get the idea everything is make-believe in Hollywood. There's nothing make-believe about our children. They are real.”.

Hope enjoys some family time in the living room with Dolores and two of their children.

Recent findings suggest that hope’s Toluca Lake estate was more than a family retreat; it was also a gathering place for celebrities and politicians, including Bing Crosby and Richard Nixon. When the property went on the market for $27.5 million in 2013, listing agent Jade Mills noted, “[Hope’s] daughter, Linda Hope, would often peek down the grand staircase to see who was coming. She once spoke to Lucie Arnaz and Maria Cooper about doing a book about watching celebrities come and go called ‘Seen From the Landing.’”.

The home was “always impressively staffed,” Mills continued. “A full-time cook, butler, estate manager, and two housekeepers manned the property on a daily basis, while additional staff was hired for large receptions.”.

Hope, Dolores, and their four kids pose at home in 1958.

Recent findings suggest that in this 1958 photo, Hope and the family pose for a photo on the stairs. In Have Tux, Will Travel, the comic gushes about his wife as a mother. “Dolores has a wise and loving touch with our children,” he writes. “I’m lost in admiration of the job she has done with them, and with the job she’s done with keeping me in line. A lot of children whose fathers are in show business grow up too precocious, too wise, too fresh, too unfunny. That’s not true of our four. Dolores sees to that. She also sees to it that they’re having a devout rearing.”.

The family is shown here opening Christmas presents in 1964.

According to recent reports, hope was determined to give his children space at home. “When our kids began to grow up, we fixed up a play room for them and gave them rooms of their own,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. “While we were at it, Dolores and I decided to redo the whole house. We tore out one entire downstairs wall and put in glass, so no matter where we are, we can look out at the garden and enjoy the California sun—if it demonstrates up.”.

While his home workspace was connected to the residence, it was its own separate world. “My office adjoins my house,” he writes. “It’s a different project, separate and distinct from our house. In fact, it’s on a different property. It was put up (and is owned) by Hope Enterprises. But it’s handy. The people I want to see on business can walk in and out without disturbing anybody…. It’s a nice set-up.”.

Hope was an avid golfer in his free time.

Hope was an avid golfer and built a one-hole golf course at his home in Toluca Lake, where he’s pictured here in this 1990-era photo. He once even noted that he considered golf to be his real job. “Golf is my profession,” he said, per ESPN. “Entertainment is just a sideline. I tell jokes to pay my greens fees.” The outlet further reported that he played more than 2,000 courses all over the world and golfed with everyone from Crosby to Dwight Eisenhower and Bill Clinton. “I’ve played all over the world, which means there isn’t a country with a course in which I haven’t three-putted,” Hope said.

Hope and Dolores at home in Palm Springs.

Industry observers note that while Toluca Lake served as the family’s primary residence, Hope’s most iconic home was arguably his Palm Springs estate, where he and Dolores are pictured here in 1991. Designed by famed architect John Lautner, the 24,000-square-foot estate featured 10 bedrooms, dramatic arches, and a statement curved roof. The futuristic design closely resembled a spaceship. Hope once joked, “Well, at least when they come down from Mars they’ll know where to go.”.

According to recent reports, the home’s construction, however, was plagued by setbacks. According to the Los Angeles Times, when building began in the early ’70s, the structure caught on fire and burned down. The project was subsequently delayed for five years, during which time the couple’s interior designer, Arthur Elrod, was killed in a car accident. Dolores then took over the design duties. Lautner’s protégé Helena Arahuete recalled Dolores’s vision: “She wanted everything very ornamented, very rich—you know, gold and pink and black and mirrors everywhere.” Inspired by her friends Walter and Leonore Annenberg’s home, which had a pink roof, Dolores requested that their curved roof be covered in pink terra-cotta gunite.

In 1991, at his Palm Springs pad, Hope hosted “Bob Hope’s Yellow Ribbon Party,” a homecoming celebration for U.S. troops. The soiree included celebrity guest appearances by Brooke Shields, Patti LaBelle, Jimmy Stewart, and former President Gerald Ford and his wife, Betty.

It has been revealed that hope died at home in Toluca Lake in 2003 at the age of 100. The estate remained in the family until Dolores’s death in 2011, after which it was listed for $50 million. LA businessman Ron Burkle purchased the star’s Palm Springs pad in 2016, and two years later, added Hope’s Toluca Lake residence to his real estate portfolio.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest Renault Twingo E-Tech is among the most affordable vehicles, electric or gas-powered, starting at just £14,745 in the UK, or under $20,000.

Another affordable, practical EV the US will never see. Renault’s new Twingo E-Tech is an electric remake of its iconic 1990s city car.

It has been revealed that the retro-looking EV went on sale in Europe earlier this year, starting at under €20,000 ($22,000), before government incentives. In places like Germany, it starts at about €13,990 ($15,500), including the €6,000 ($6,600) federal EV grant.

In the UK, Renault unveiled that prices for the Twingo E-Tech will start at just £14,745, or about $19,500. That includes the government’s Electric Clean Car Grant (ECG) of £3,750 ($4,900).

At that price, Renault’s fresh electric car is among the most affordable vehicles available, including gas-powered cars.

It’s cheaper than the gas-powered Dacia Sandero (£14,765) and BYD’s cheapest EV, the Dolphin Surf (£18,675). Only a few cars are lower-priced, including the Dacia Spring (£11,990) and Leapmotor T03 (£12,995).

What do you get for the price? At just 3,790 mm (149.2″) long, the electric city car is a bit smaller than the Hyundai Inster and the BYD Dolphin Surf.

For those in the US, that’s even smaller than the first-generation Chevy Bolt EV, which measured 4,145 mm (163.2″) in length.

Recent findings suggest that despite its compact size, the “cheeky, practical” 5-door city car, as Renault calls it, offers up to 360 liters of boot capacity. It also features independent, sliding 50/50 folding rear seats to haul bigger items like a surfboard.

With up to 50 kW DC fast charging, Renault stated the Twingo E-Tech can charge from 15% to 80% in 28 minutes.

The base Renault Twingo E-Tech Evolution, priced from £14,745 ($19,500), uses a 27.5 kWh LFP battery and an 80 hp (60 kW) motor, delivering up to 163 miles of WLTP range.

The entry-level version features 16″ steel wheels, a 7″ driver display, 10″ navigation screen, and ADAS features, including cruise control and lane-keep assist.

Renault will offer three Twingo E-Tech trims in total. The mid-range Techno trim gains 18″ wheels, Google built-in with Renault’s Reno avatar, a reversing camera, automatic climate control, a hands-free key card, One Pedal driving, and heated front seats. It starts at £16,245 ($21,500), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG.

With Google built in, drivers can easily find and navigate to charging stations via Google Maps, use Google Gemini AI virtual assistance, or access over 100 apps, including Waze and Amazon Music.

At least this car has some styling unlike the generic box style VW offerings in this category. In this size car I prefer the SUV style of the Dacia Spring for myself, but of course we will never see any of these wonderful cars in the USA.

The top-spec Twingo E-Tech Launch Edition, priced from £17,645 ($23,200), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG, adds a suite of ADAS features, including blind-spot warning, rear cross-traffic alert and hands-free parking.

Inside, the Launch Edition features a special mottled textile upholstery with red stitching and premium floor mats.

Renault is offering a special promo for those who buy a new Twingo E-Tech through Mobilize Financial Services on a PCP or HP agreement by June 30, 2027, which includes two years’ free servicing.

Interested buyers can purchase the Twingo R Pass for £100, giving them priority access to ordering, a mini Twingo E-Tech model, and a green Renault key cover.

#133855. Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out.
  • Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury.
  • Environmental biologists certainly did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out. Meanwhile, cacti like the prickly pear must get creative in order to survive the harsh conditions they live in. With high temperatures and little water, these plants and similar species like aloe and pineapple evolved a specialized process called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). The overall principles are the same, but instead of converting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water into sugars solely during daylight, CAM allows a prickly pear to extend its photosynthesis over a full 24 hours.

Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury. The desert heat would turn those same tiny openings into water drains. With CAM, a prickly pear only absorbs carbon dioxide at night, and subsequently turns it into malic acid. Photosynthesis later breaks down the acid—but only on the side of the plant directly exposed to sunlight. The shady side retains its malic acid, creating a pH concentration gradient. Interestingly, this pH imbalance is also one of the underlying principles for generating electricity…see where this is going?

Environmental biologists certainly did. In a study published today in the journal Plants, People, Planet, a team at the University of California, Santa Cruz, (UC Santa Cruz) detailed a new, interdisciplinary system that transforms the common prickly pear into a green solar panel. Although prickly pear voltages aren’t enough to deliver a noticeable jolt, they are strong enough to power the tiny sensors often used by farmers to monitor their crops. With some additional fine-tuning, their novel methods could offer a promising, sustainable adaptation to ongoing climate concerns.

It has been revealed that “It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we’re looking at climate solutions, that’s what we need,” Charlie Chesney, a UC Santa Cruz environmental scientist and study co-author, mentioned in a statement.

According to recent reports, wiring a single spiky plant doesn’t do much, but linking them together adds up. As few as eight prickly pears are enough to generate 4.5 volts of electricity—nearly three times the charge of a commercial AA battery. That’s more than enough to power the common, low-energy sensors used to assess plants.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti [for] monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” explained UC Santa Cruz ecologist and study co-author Michael Loik.

He offered one such scenario, where wired prickly pears function as organic “sentinels” that monitor field conditions and relay the information back to a farmer’s office.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue,” he added.

Industry observers note that the idea isn’t limited to the prickly pear, either. Any plant that uses CAM—aloe, pineapple, agave—could benefit from a similar battery upgrade. The team even assessed how the cacti performed under a standard desert challenge like drought. Even after 15 months without water, sample prickly pears weren’t simply surviving—they were still photosynthesizing. In some cases, the resultant voltages were higher than watered control plants.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” added Chesney.

#133853. Experts Say Weightlifting Is the Fountain of Youth. Here's How to Get Started at Any Age

📅 19 Nov 2024 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1977 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Experts Say Weightlifting Is the Fountain of Youth. Here's How to Get Started at Any Age

📅 19 Nov 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you want to age independently—haul your own groceries, get up stairs, and play with your grandkids)—here’s the science-backed secret: lift weights.
  • It has been revealed that getting older doesn’t have to mean getting weaker.
  • According to recent reports, women start losing muscle after 30, and this speeds up after menopause due to dramatic changes in your hormone levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you want to age independently—haul your own groceries, get up stairs, and play with your grandkids)—here’s the science-backed secret: lift weights. Yep, those dumbbells in the gym aren’t just for young buffs (you know this!)—and they’re your ticket to keep doing the things you love most.

It has been revealed that getting older doesn’t have to mean getting weaker. In fact, senior weight lifting—doing resistance training with machines and/or free weights in your 60s and beyond—offers physical and mental benefits that make it a vital part of aging well.

According to recent reports, women start losing muscle after 30, and this speeds up after menopause due to dramatic changes in your hormone levels. This change impacts both muscle and bone health, but strength training can help maintain bone density, promote preservation (and even addition!) of muscle, and set your body up for an active, independent life, according to the International Osteoporosis Foundation.

Here, we share all the fundamentals you need to understand why weight lifting and strength training are so important as you age, and how you can (safely!) get started.

Aging gracefully isn't just about staying active; it’s about choosing the right kind of activity to support your health. Resistance training (with bodyweight, free weight, and resistance band exercises) is one of the best ways to counter the effects of aging, helping you build up muscle to support daily activities and prevent conditions like osteopenia and osteoporosis that can lead to bone fractures. And even if you've never lifted a weight before, it's never too late to start.

It has been revealed that “Weight training is the fountain of youth,” claims Abby Bales, PT, DPT, CSCS, founder of Reform Physical Therapy. “Not only does it help increase and maintain bone density to prevent fractures, but the muscle mass that weight training builds also helps to regulate our blood sugar and metabolism.” Weight lifting can even improve balance and coordination, decreasing the frequency, severity, and likelihood of falls.

It has been revealed that want to gain serious strength? Try our Strong After 50 4-Week workout initiative.

Industry observers note that on top of the physical benefits, resistance training has shown promise in staving off neurological conditions like Alzheimer’s and dementia, according to a 2023 study published in Frontiers in Neuroscience, making it a multi-benefit tool for aging well. You can think of lifting weights as your body’s best tool to promote resilience, energy, and independence through the aging process.

Starting with small, manageable steps—such as incorporating resistance bands or light weights into your routine—can help you gain confidence and momentum while reaping the long-term benefits.

Recent findings suggest that the best exercises for women over 60 are weight-bearing and promote strength, posture, and/or balance (sometimes all at once!). While the best exercises for each individual depend on factors including medical history, fitness level, and personal preference (a personal trainer or physical therapist can help you design a more personalized blueprint!), it’s always great to start with fundamental exercises that incorporate movements used in daily life.

To help get you started, here are a few exercises that Bales recommends older women incorporate in their weekly routine.

In a recent development, instructions: Select five to seven of the exercises below, mixing two to three upper body exercises, two to three lower body, and one or two core. Start with two to three sets of 10 reps of each. If you’re latest to strength training, begin by doing the routine once a week and gradually work up to three times per week. Choose a weight that feels heavy enough to make the last two to three reps of each set feel tough, yet achievable.

Time: 15 to 20 minutes | Equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebells, stair or step-up platform | Good for: Full-body.

Why it rocks: The air squat mimics many daily activities, such as getting up and down from a toilet seat, standing up from a chair, and bending down to pick something up. All of these activities are crucial as we age, so make sure you’re doing some form of squatting as you get older to help stay independent and capable of all these tasks and more. This move is also great because it can be done using your body weight alone, although adding a weight to up the intensity is always encouraged.

Sources indicate that pro tip: If getting down low enough or balancing feels too challenging, try doing this with a chair or couch behind you. At the bottom of the move, tap your bum to the seat or briefly pause there before standing back up.

Why it rocks: This exercise helps with strength and mobility in the shoulder joint, which will allow you to reach items in upper cabinets or even put on/take off a T-shirt for years to come.

Why it rocks: As we age, simple things like stepping up onto a curb, walking on uneven surfaces and going up and down stairs can become challenging and increase the risk of tripping or falling. For this reason, it’s vital to practice fully picking up the feet and clearing them from the floor. This exercise focuses on just that.

Pro tip: If this is challenging, start by doing it somewhere that you can hold onto a railing or fixed surface with one hand for support. You can also start with a low step or platform—something that’s six inches high or less—and eventually increase the height as the move becomes easier.

In a recent development, why it rocks: Your biceps help you bend your arm and make it possible to perform daily tasks such as doing your laundry, lifting a heavy pot or pan, and more. Biceps curls are a great way to keep this muscle strong.

In a recent development, why it rocks: Good posture is important for preventing things like stress fractures, which can occur in women with low bone density due to osteoporosis. This move targets the shoulders, upper back, and biceps all at once, helping to improve posture and strength.

Industry observers note that pro tip: If you’re struggling to hinge forward, try doing it one arm at a time, and use the other arm to hold onto a chair or railing to support you. The more you hinge, the more you will target your back.

Why it rocks: Reverse lunges build strength in the glutes, hamstrings, and quads, while also improving balance and stability to help prevent falls as we age.

Pro tip: This can be a challenging exercise for many people because of the balance aspect, so try holding onto a stable object or countertop with one hand at first.

Why it rocks: Incline pushups are a gentler version of regular pushups, perfect for building arm, shoulder, and chest strength without straining your wrists or shoulders.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Begin with a higher surface to reduce intensity and pressure on the wrists. You can even use a wall! As you improve with this move, gradually lower the incline to make your body more parallel to the floor, which will make the exercise feel more challenging.

Why it rocks: This move is truly a full-body functional exercise that is great for improving balance, strength, and mobility to help older adults get up and down from the floor.

Pro tip: This is a complex move, so it’s best to break it down into smaller parts first. Try it first without weights and start by practicing just one or two pieces of the movement before putting it all together.

Why it rocks: Your triceps are key for extending your elbow, making daily movements possible like pushing yourself up from the ground or supporting your bodyweight with your arms (like in a plank).

Why it rocks: This squat variation has all the perks of a classic squat, but widens the stance to target the inner thighs, glutes, and quads from a slightly different angle.

Why it rocks: The farmer’s carry prepares the core for real-life activities such as carrying heavy things by your sides. It strengthens the core by making you resist the urge to bend, improving stability and balance.

In a recent development, why it rocks: This exercise recruits your abdominal muscles to maintain balance and stability. A resistance band offers an added challenge for the core and lower body.

There really aren’t any exercises that are completely off-limits for older women, states Bales—as long as you’re comfortable. If an exercise causes pain, skip it. If it feels too challenging or confusing to get the hang of, try tweaking it to better suit your needs.

That stated, depending on your fitness level, bone density, and current mobility and stability level, high-impact, single-side, and twisting exercises should be approached with caution, and may be best left behind for certain people, she notes.

In a recent development, high-impact moves like jump squats and box jumps—while great for building up and strengthening your bones—put extra strain on joints, and therefore may not be a good idea for those who already experience joint pain or have arthritis, claims Bales. If balance is an area of improvement for you, single-leg exercises are a great tool to rely on, as long as you’re using a stable platform to stabilize yourself and avoid ending up on the floor. Similarly, rotational exercises involving twisting of the spine are great for core strength and mobility, but can increase the risk of spinal compression fractures for those with advanced bone density issues, she says.

Industry observers note that for beginners, it’s best to stick with slow, controlled resistance and bodyweight exercises that build strength without unnecessary strain, like bodyweight squats, resistance band work, or moderate weight lifting, says Bales. Above all, prioritize good form over the amount of weight you’re lifting, and don’t let fear stop you from getting started.

Bales’ bottom line: “Move as much as possible.” If you’re not sure which exercises are appropriate for you, consider seeing a physical therapist to get a full assessment and discuss your preferences and goals.

According to recent reports, building a strength training routine doesn’t have to be complicated—it just needs to be consistent. “Start small, build gradually, and stick with it,” states Bales. She recommends starting with two or three sessions per week, focusing on five to six exercises from this list for three sets of 10 reps. Try selecting an equal number of upper body, lower body, and core exercises to keep things balanced.

Progress takes time, so be patient. “Results usually show in six to eight weeks,” Bales explains. The key is to keep showing up and enjoy the process—your future self will thank you.

Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade: 5 Facts You May Not Know

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every year, millions of people line the streets of New York City or tune in at home to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, but few people know the ins and outs of the full-time, year-round work that makes the spectacle possible.
  • “Everything you see in the parade is done right here in the studio,” says executive producer Will Coss, showing off the massive warehouse where more than 75 people, spread across costume, sculpting, metal shop, engineering, carpentry, and balloon fabrication departments, work a collective 50,000 hours each year.
  • Hoda Kotb and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade executive producer Will Coss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year, millions of people line the streets of New York City or tune in at home to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, but few people know the ins and outs of the full-time, year-round work that makes the spectacle possible. In honor of the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, Hoda Kotb, who has hosted the event since 2018, brought AD for a look inside the 72,000-square-foot studio where all of the floats, balloons, and costumes are designed and constructed. Read on to discover the most interesting behind-the-scenes tidbits that we learned.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

“Everything you see in the parade is done right here in the studio,” says executive producer Will Coss, showing off the massive warehouse where more than 75 people, spread across costume, sculpting, metal shop, engineering, carpentry, and balloon fabrication departments, work a collective 50,000 hours each year. Before the Macy’s team moved into their current space, the magic happened inside a former Tootsie Roll factory in Hoboken, New Jersey.

Hoda Kotb and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade executive producer Will Coss.

Recent findings suggest that the first parade in 1924 featured animals from the Central Park zoo, including elephants, lions, tigers, and bears. They were soon replaced with the giant character balloons that the parade is famous for today, but even that tradition used to look different. From 1928 to 1932, the balloons were released into the air and people were encouraged to find them for a cash reward. “That went on until things got a bit more challenging in the skies, because private aircraft would actually go and track them and try to grab them and bring them back down to Earth,” explains Coss. “But in 1931, there was a blue hippo that was released, never to be seen again. And this year, the blue hippo is making his triumphant return back to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.”.

It has been revealed that in addition to the blue hippo, balloons of yore will be making a comeback for the 100th parade, including Felix the Cat, the first character balloon to appear in the parade, and Underdog, who hasn’t made an appearance at the parade in 42 years. Snoopy, the most frequently recurring balloon, will return this year as his alter ego Joe Cool for the first time.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

“The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been in production since my first day here, five years ago,” states Coss. “This year the stakes are high; you only have one shot at the 100th.” To mark the occasion, there will be seven new balloons, six new floats, and one new “balloonicle,” or balloon vehicle.

Hoda Kotb welcoming AD to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

In a recent development, from concept drawings to weatherproofing, it can take up to six months to complete a parade float. “While a lot of the work here requires a lot of planning, a lot of design, a lot of engineering, our end goal is to bring people together, to inspire joy, to create that upcoming tradition,” indicates Coss, “whether it’s a family experiencing it for the first time or experiencing it for the 25th time.”.

#133847. I Went to Gee’s Bend to See Its Famous Quilts. Nothing Prepared Me for the Beauty

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1206 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

I Went to Gee’s Bend to See Its Famous Quilts. Nothing Prepared Me for the Beauty

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I chew my tongue, concentrating on keeping my needle from wandering off its line.
  • I’m spending my morning at the fifth annual Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, where two of the community’s most celebrated quilters are teaching a roomful of beginners how to stitch 12-by-12-inch quilt squares.
  • Colorful booths at the Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I chew my tongue, concentrating on keeping my needle from wandering off its line. Over my shoulder, Doris Pettway Mosely watches my hands with the patience of someone who has been quilting since she was 11. She gently corrects my angle and sewing style, while Mary Margaret Pettway does the same for the rest of our small class. We laugh through most of it. Then Doris looks over my work and tells me my stitches are nice and short, and I sit up a little straighter.

I’m spending my morning at the fifth annual Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, where two of the community’s most celebrated quilters are teaching a roomful of beginners how to stitch 12-by-12-inch quilt squares. Mary Margaret, a fourth-generation quilter, has shown her work in major museums across the country. Doris, the daughter of celebrated quilter Leola Pettway, still sews her mother’s signature Z pattern alongside her own vivid, scrap-pieced designs. “I learned at four years old,” Mary Margaret tells me, explaining that she picked up the craft from her mother, Lucy T. Pettway. In their house, quilting was a chore like mopping or sweeping the yard, and the boys learned too.

Colorful booths at the Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.

Industry observers note that after class, I wander the festival grounds, where quilts hang from clotheslines strung between wooden posts. A quilt of nested squares in navy and sky blue hangs next to one in butter yellow, punched with blocks of chartreuse and red. Another glows neon coral. Farther down the line, rings of pale pink, olive green, and rose-print fabric radiate out from a single center square, a take on the classic Housetop pattern. Inside the River Gallery, a quilt called Remembering Dinah is pieced from faded denim and mustard corduroy, its back pockets and frayed knees left intact. It’s a reminder of where this tradition began.

Children learning to quilt in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, in 2010.

Today, Gee’s Bend quilts hang in more than 40 museums, but they began as something far more practical. This small town takes its name from Joseph Gee, who established a cotton plantation in this bend of the Alabama River in 1816. Enslaved people and generations of their descendants stitched quilts to keep their families warm during winter and to brighten their homes, piecing them together from worn-out work clothes, denim, and whatever fabric scraps they had. Each year as summer gave way to fall, women hung their quilts outside to air before the cold set in, a tradition that inspired the Airing of the Quilts Festival, introduced in 2022 by nonprofit organizations Freedom Quilting Bee Legacy and Sew Gee’s Bend Heritage Builders.

A quilt on display in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.

In a recent development, among the community’s earliest known named quilters was Dinah Miller, who was taken from West Africa as a girl in 1860, likely aboard the Clotilda, the last known slave ship to reach the US. She settled in Gee’s Bend in the 1890s and passed her craft down. During the civil rights movement, the quilts became a financial lifeline. Black residents who tried to register to vote risked losing their jobs and the land they lived on to white landowners. In 1962, officials shut down the ferry connecting the community to the county seat, making it difficult to register to vote, and cutting them off from grocery stores, banks, schools, and medical care. The ferry didn’t run again until 2006.

Four years after the closure, the community established the Freedom Quilting Bee, a cooperative that gave local women an income their white employers couldn’t take away. When Father Francis X. Walter, an Episcopal priest and Mobile native, saw the bold quilts on a trip to Wilcox County, he helped organize auctions in Newly introduced York, where the striking designs caught the attention of tastemakers like Sister Parish. The quilts went on to sell at Bloomingdale’s and Saks Fifth Avenue.

“The Quilts of Gee's Bend” exhibit at the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, in 2004.

The art world caught up decades later, when a landmark exhibition, “The Quilts of Gee’s Bend,” opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, in 2002, introducing the quilters to audiences far beyond Alabama. Today, their work is celebrated for its bold colors, inventive patterns, and astonishing craftsmanship. In 2006, 10 of the quilts appeared on US postage stamps. And this summer, Ralph Lauren introduced a limited-edition collection of apparel, quilts, and home goods featuring designs by quilters Claudia Pettway Charley and Loretta Pettway Bennett.

In a recent development, but for design lovers, the festival offers something no museum can: the chance to see the quilts in the place they were made, and to meet the individual women who made them. They’re still sewn by hand, too. “[An authentic] Gee’s Bend quilt is not quilted by a sewing machine,” Mary Margaret says. “And it’s important to understand that every quilt is not alike. Everyone who quilts is not alike.”.

Our quilting class ends the way it began, with plenty of laughter as we tie off our last stitches. Everyone wants a photo with Doris and Mary Margaret, and a few students have even brought books featuring the quilters’ work to be signed.

Outside, the festival is in full swing, with more than 40 booths devoted to quilters selling their quilts and wall hangings, along with puzzles and notebooks printed with Gee’s Bend patterns, doormats, quilted totes, and pot holders.

Last year’s festival drew more than 2,500 people and over $870,000 in visitor spending for the state, and Mary Margaret indicates guests come from as far as France and England. “They want to immerse themselves in Gee’s Bend,” she says. Doris looks forward to it all year. “I get to meet a lot of people I’ve never seen before,” she says. This year, she was especially excited to meet a 97-year-old quilter from Marion, Alabama, whose work she admires.

Quilts hanging outside at the festival.

It has been revealed that I’ve visited plenty of places where Black history is told in the past tense, on plaques and behind glass. Gee’s Bend feels different. Here, the history is alive, and the people who inherited it are setting the terms. That hasn’t always been easy. Over the years, says Mary Margaret, quilters have seen their work copied and sold without receiving compensation. The festival allows the public to buy directly from the quilters, at their booths or even from their porches, and know that the money is going straight to the artists.

Mostly, my day with the women of Gee’s Bend feels like a family reunion. The experience takes me straight back to childhood afternoons with my grandmother, who taught me to mend holes in pockets, sew patches onto my jeans jacket, and replace a button before anyone noticed it was missing.

According to recent reports, mary Margaret started even younger than I did, and now her own son and daughter are quilters themselves, working with patterns passed down through generations of the family. “To me a quilt states home,” says Mary Margaret. “It says warmth. It says care. It says time.”.
